title: Joy is your strength (Nehemiah 8:10)
hookLine: "the joy of the LORD is your strength"; eat, drink and send portions

cards: The crowd is crying. All morning they've stood in the street and listened, and now that the words have been explained, they understand them.
The text says it plainly: all the people wept when they heard the words of the law. Maybe they're hearing how far they've drifted. Maybe it's the weight of a whole people coming home.
The book only says they wept. And then their leaders, Nehemiah, Ezra and the Levites, do something unexpected. They don't tell them to cry harder.

teach.h: THIS DAY IS HOLY. DON'T WEEP.
teach.b: This day is holy to the LORD your God, they say; don't mourn, and don't weep. Then comes an instruction that sounds like a party invitation.

In the King James words: "Go your way, eat the fat, and drink the sweet, and send portions unto them for whom nothing is prepared: for this day is holy unto our LORD: neither be ye sorry; for the joy of the LORD is your strength."
Eat the rich food. Drink the sweet drink. And send portions to the people who have nothing ready.
The joy isn't private; it goes out the door on a plate.

teach.h: THE JOY OF THE LORD IS YOUR STRENGTH.
teach.b: The Hebrew word for strength here is ma'oz, and some readers hear in it a stronghold, a place of refuge. On that reading, joy isn't only a feeling of being strong; it's a place to stand.
Joy as a wall, in a book about building walls. The Levites quiet the people: hold your peace, for the day is holy; don't be grieved.

And the people go off to eat and drink, send portions and make great rejoicing, the text says, because they had understood the words that were declared to them. The tears came from understanding, and so did the joy.
Readers of the book of Esther may hear an echo here: Purim, too, is kept with feasting and with sending portions one to another.

how: Jewish festivals are kept with festive meals, and on Purim it is the custom to send gifts of food to friends and give to the poor, as the book of Esther describes.

games.q: what does “joy is your strength” mean?
o: a command to hide sadness and smile anyway
a promise that happy people never get sick
joy in God as a place to stand, shared with others

games.q: the day at the water gate — tap the pairs.

s: the leaders told the people to keep weeping
they said the day is holy: don't mourn, don't weep, go and eat.
the people rejoiced because they had understood the words
the text gives that as the reason for their great rejoicing.
Nehemiah's feast was only for the people already at the table
he says to send portions to those for whom nothing is prepared.

games.q: you're one of the leaders. the crowd has just understood the teaching, and they're all in tears. what do you tell them?
o: go home quietly and think it over.
this day is holy: eat, drink, and send portions.
games.why: "go your way, eat the fat, and drink the sweet, and send portions... for the joy of the LORD is your strength."

practice: Bring to mind one good thing from this week, and let yourself enjoy remembering it.
Then think of someone for whom nothing is prepared, a neighbor who eats alone, a friend having a hard month, and picture the portion you'd send them, a meal, a coffee, a plate from your own table.
If you pray, give thanks for the good thing in words from your tradition.

wordCard.voice: Joy is your strength. The people stop weeping, eat and drink, and send portions to those with nothing, because the joy of the LORD is their strength. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: joy, gladness, the word for joy in Nehemiah 8:10.

carryVoice: Your line: joy is your strength. On a holy day, the table sets a second plate. Until tomorrow.
